# THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE IRREALIS: A LEXICOGRAPHICAL PALIMPSEST

### *From the Bureau of Suspended Predicates, Oublière-sur-Charente*
#### *Codex Expurget: Reg. IX (Fascicles of the Westward Nave)*
*Master Scribe Elian Vane, Primus Archon recensens*

---

```
================================================================================
DIRECTORATE EXPURGET INDEX: ITEM 771-B
Root: †Velle-charentis (v. irr., defect.)
Inflection Redacted: Coniunctivus Potentialis [Third-Tier Hypothetical]
Structural Counterpart: The Transverse Ribs of the Westward Clerestory (Vaulting 14–19)
Phonetic Vector: Open-throat posterior fricative /x/ trailing into high-register optative /ø̃/
Acoustic Consequence: Immediate desiccation of ambient chamber resonance; 
                      settling of load-bearing calcarenite by 4.2 centimeters per deleted mood.
Decree: Let the dependent clause be excised from the liturgical ledger with the dry scraper; 
        let no mason whisper the conditions under which the arch might have held.
================================================================================
```

---

### FASCICLE I: THE SCAFFOLDING OF THE UNOCCURRED

Had it been granted to me, in that final, unseasonable autumn before the Lexical Directorate walled up the acoustic conduits of the lower cloisters, to foresee how the slow, systematic butchery of our subordinate syntax would leave not merely the city’s libraries but its very parapets destitute of balance, I should perhaps have dipped my horn in vitriol rather than oak-gall, so that every codex entrusted to my pumice might have dissolved into ash rather than submit to this clinical, petrifying butchery. 

For thirty years, we who climbed the spiral ascents of the Scriptorium of the Westward Nave understood that our limestone was not inert matter drawn from the damp bowels of the Charente, but an externalized, lithic cartilage sustained exclusively by the suspension of resolution—that is to say, by the magnificent, soaring architecture of the *irrealis*. When a mason cut a voussoir for an arch spanning sixty feet of empty air, he did not rely upon the vulgar, terrestrial brute-force of compression alone; he sang into the setting-mortar the ancient, hypotactic sequences of the *Coniunctivus Potentialis*, intoning those labyrinthine clauses of possibility (*“were the earth to yield beneath the footing, yet would this stone refuse the center”*) which held the travertine in perpetual, weightless contemplation of its own fall. 

```
[Marginalia: E.V. — transcribed in clandestine charcoal, 0.2mm micro-script]
    ...and yet, Mireille, were you to have stepped from the quay five seconds 
    earlier, or had I not lingered to adjust the copper catch of my satchel 
    (that satchel which contained, irony of ironies, the unexpurgated grammar 
    of the Fourth Subjunctive), your hem would not have caught upon the mooring-iron. 
    The water was not deep; it was merely indifferent. I tell myself each dawn 
    that if the current had been swifter, my hesitation would have signified nothing. 
    To hesitate in the indicative is cowardice; to hesitate in the irrealis 
    is an infinite cathedral of alternative mercies...
```

Now, under the iron-tipped scrapers of the Directorate, the city shrinks to the dimensions of an abattoir. As I sit at my cedar desk, positioned precisely beneath the southern rose window—whose stone tracery now weeps a fine, powdery dust of pulverized dolomite whenever the wind forces an unapproved subjunctive through the mullions—I am commanded to execute the *mandatum praecisum*. I draw the *rasorium* across the vellum. 

The rule is mercilessly simple: wherever a sentence branches into what *might have been*, into the tender, verdant meadows of the counterfactual where the soul wanders among uncommitted sins and unfallen spires, the blade must descend. I pare away the prefix *an-* (marking the past optative); I scrape the parchment until the skin is translucent as the membrane of an unborn calf; I brush the scraped ink-dust into the leaden urn at my knees.

Directly beneath my sandals, thirty feet down in the vaulted hollow of the Nave, a sharp, dry sound—like the snapping of a dry thigh-bone in winter—echoes through the nave.

A fissure has opened in the fourteenth transverse rib. The keystone, suddenly deprived of the linguistic tension that reasoned it into suspension, has dropped an eighth of an inch. The stone knows. The stone has forgotten how to hope.

---

```
================================================================================
DIRECTORATE EXPURGET INDEX: ITEM 814-D
Root: †Miserari-si (v. impers., optat.)
Inflection Redacted: Irrealis Praeteriti [The Counterfactual of Unconsummated Calamity]
Structural Counterpart: The Flying Buttresses of the North Aisle (Pier-Stems VII through XII)
Phonetic Vector: Nasalized dental stop /d̪/ dissolving into the unvoiced glottal sigh /h/
Spatial Diagnosis: Reduction of interior cubic volume by lateral displacement of the arcade.
Decree: The memory of that which did not occur is an economic surplus yielding no civic tithe. 
        Strike the conditional particle *olam* from all municipal registers.
================================================================================
```

---

### FASCICLE II: THE ARCHITRAVES OF DOUBT

To live in Oublière-sur-Charente during the Great Expungement is to inhabit a mind whose rooms are being bricked up from within by a mason who works without a plumb-line. One awakens to find that the street outside one’s window, which yesterday curved with a graceful, speculative sweep toward the river—as if inviting the pedestrian to consider whether he might prefer the shadow of the willow-walk to the dust of the tannery—has snapped into a rigid, terrifyingly straight line of gravel. The houses, whose upper stories once leaned across the cobbles toward one another in an intimate, optative colloquy, have retracted their gables, standing flush and dead-eyed, strictly indicative, admitting no light save that which can be measured by the surveyor’s chain.

I have begun to lose the names for my own grief. 

When I look at the small tin daguerreotype I keep hidden within the hollowed heel of my left boot, the face that looks back at me is blurred, not merely by the primitive chemistry of the plate, but by the systematic eradication of the lexical bridges that once connected my present self to that sodden afternoon. 

Was her name Mireille? 

In the archaic Vesperine dialect, the name *Mireille* is derived from the middle-voice participle of *mirari*, but inflected through the optative suffix *-eille*, signifying *“she whom one might eternally have contemplated with wonder, had the light not failed.”* If I excise the suffix—as the Director, Arch-Censor Malquoir, stood over my shoulder and forced me to do this morning to the fourteenth-century Antiphonary of St. Jude-in-the-Fens—does the woman herself evaporate from the registry of being?

```
[Marginalia: E.V. — script showing erratic tremor; ink thinned with vinegar]
    ...My hand shook as Malquoir watched. The iron nib tore the vellum. 
    Underneath the erased line, the ghost of the letter remained: the twin loops 
    of the optative liquid consonant. I tasted river-silt in my mouth. 
    I asked myself: Did I see her drown, or did I merely read of a drowning 
    in a romance composed in the high hypothetical style of the Second Dynasty? 
    If I say: "She drowned," the statement possesses the flat, dead weight of an anvil. 
    If I am permitted to write: "She might have lived, had the sluice-keeper 
    not mistaken the vesper bell," then an entire universe of air and water 
    and breathing lung-tissue opens like a fan. 
    Malquoir said: "You are daydreaming, Archon. The knife is dull. Hone it."
```

The physical city does not merely mirror our grammar; it is its acoustic accumulator. Bachelard was wrong only in this: the house does not hold its memories in its cellar like preserved fruit; the cellar *is* the memory’s grammatical case. When we destroy the counterfactual, we destroy the spatial buffer between the human animal and the sheer, crushing mass of dead matter. 

This afternoon, the mason-guilds were seen carrying away the statues of the *Seven Speculations* from the western portal. These figures had no faces—they possessed only stone hands turned outward in gestures of perpetual qualification: the thumb tucked slightly beneath the forefinger, indicating *“perchance”*; the wrist cocked at forty-five degrees, denoting *“unless otherwise decreed.”* 

As the iron chains dragged the third statue down onto the flagstones, its head severed on the curb. A low, hollow hum rose from the limestone paving—a subterranean vibration that traveled up through the soles of my shoes and settled in my teeth. It was the fundamental resonant frequency of the city losing its third harmonic. Without the hypothetical, the limestone cannot distribute its load; it becomes brittle, vitreous, prone to sudden, catastrophic cleavage.

My left eye has begun to twitch in rhythm with the falling keystones. When I close it, I see only blank, whitewashed parchment. When I open it, the world has lost another layer of distance. The distant hills beyond the river, which used to shimmer in a haze of conjunctive blue, appear painted upon the very glass of the window-pane, flat as a theatrical flat, pressing their raw chalk edges against my forehead.

---

```
================================================================================
DIRECTORATE EXPURGET INDEX: ITEM 902-A
Root: †Essere-absens (v. subst., defective-optative)
Inflection Redacted: Perfect Irrealis of the Unattained Self [The "I-that-was-not"]
Structural Counterpart: The Lantern Tower and the Intercolumniation of the Apse
Phonetic Vector: Pure unvoiced sibilant /s/ accompanied by sudden glottal closure
Linguistic Impact: Total obsolescence of remorse, nostalgia, and speculative self-critique.
Decree: Henceforth, all citizens exist only in the mode of absolute presence. 
        The phrase "I should have been" is replaced by the formula "I am not."
================================================================================
```

---

### FASCICLE III: THE SHEARING OF THE SUBORDINATES

The work goes faster now. It must. The winter solstice approaches, and with it, the scheduled demolition of the Westward Nave. The Directorate maintains that the Nave is structurally compromised—a lie that possesses its own vile, self-fulfilling logic. The Nave is falling precisely because we have scraped sixty-four thousand square leagues of conditional discourse from its foundation charters. We are murdering the mother to harvest her shroud.

My pen no longer glides; it stumbles. The ink itself seems to have thickened, curdled by the cold that sweeps unobstructed through the gaps in the clerestory where the stained glass has dropped out. The glass did not break from the wind; it fell because the lead cames, fashioned in the seventeenth century according to complex geometric ratios derived from the *Optativus Dubitativus*, simply relaxed their grip when the clergy ceased to recite the *Nunc Dimittis* with its proper conditional clauses.

```
[Marginalia: E.V. — written with an iron stylus directly into the cedar wood of the desk]
    I cannot recall if she was fair or dark. 
    When I reach for the image of her face, my mind produces only a grammatical rule: 
    "The feminine noun takes the ablative of separation when accompanied by the verb 'to lose.'" 
    Is she dead? No. To say "she is dead" implies that she once lived in the indicative. 
    Perhaps she was only a subordinate clause I invented during my second year 
    at the Academy to balance an awkward period in my treatise on the Charente dikes. 
    If I invented her, then my grief is merely a stylistic solecism. 
    If I did not invent her, why can I not find her name in the parish roll of 
    the parish of St. Sulpice-the-Drowned? 
    The parish roll has been cleansed. 
    There are no drowned persons in the roll. 
    There are only persons who are absent. 
    Presence. Absence. 
    One. Zero. 
    The knife scrapes the wood.
```

The syntax of my daily reports to Malquoir is drying up like puddles after a north wind. Last month, I wrote: 

> *“Although one might reasonably contend that the preservation of the marginal glosses in Codex B could provide the philologist with invaluable testimonies regarding the historical transition of the dialect, it would nevertheless appear more prudent to defer their destruction until the completion of the general inventory.”*

This morning, my hand, moving under the dull, hypnotic compulsion of the Directorate’s new style-manual, produced only this:

> *“Codex B contains errors. The errors are removed. The work proceeds.”*

The world contractures. When one cannot say *“if,”* the horizon ceases to be an invitation; it becomes a fence. The citizens in the street below move with a strange, heavy, mechanical gait, their boots striking the cobbles with the unyielding, percussive thud of cast iron. They do not look up at the Nave. They do not look down at the river. They do not turn their heads at the crossroads to consider which path might offer the easier ascent. There is only one path. It is the path upon which their boots are currently placed. 

The Great Inundation thirty years ago—did it happen? 

If I am forbidden to ask how the town might have been spared had the dikes been raised by two cubits, then the Inundation was not a disaster; it was merely an altitude of the water. Disaster requires a standard of comparison; it requires that we hold in our minds two simultaneous, competing architectures—the city that stood dry upon its hill, and the city whose streets were churned to yellow foam. Expunge the hypothetical city, and the drowned child is not a tragedy; she is merely an object that has ceased to displace air.

I hear a groan from the lantern tower. It is not a metaphor. It is the friction of three thousand tons of limestone realizing that its load-bearing calculations were based upon a prepositional phrase that has just been struck from Page 412 of the Municipal Charter.

The stone does not fall all at once. It hesitates. It searches the air for the missing grammar. 

It finds nothing.

---

```
================================================================================
DIRECTORATE EXPURGET INDEX: ITEM 999-FINAL
Root: †Sperare (v. defect., absolute eradication)
Inflection Redacted: All moods, voices, and tenses non-coincident with the instant of utterance.
Structural Counterpart: The Scriptorium Floor; The Archon’s Spine; The City Wall.
Phonetic Vector: Nil. (Silence).
Decree: The work is concluded. The city is identical to itself.
================================================================================
```

---

### FASCICLE IV: THE INDICATIVE MONOLITH

The desk is cold. 

The window is gone. A sheet of gray lead covers the opening. The light does not enter; it stops at the lead.

I have the scraper. I have the parchment.

There are no marginalia. The margins are cut off. The shears were large. They cut the margins from the pages. The margins fell into the lead bucket. The porter carried the bucket away.

I sit.

I scrape.

The word is *Mireille*. 

I do not know this word. It has seven letters. It has no meaning in the civic vocabulary. It has the shape of a river reed, but it is not a reed. It is ink on calfskin.

I place the iron edge against the first letter. The *M* has two peaks. Like the gables of two houses that stood before the street was straightened. 

I press the iron. The ink turns to powder. The powder is black. It falls upon my sleeve.

Now the *M* is gone. There is only a white scar on the skin.

Now the *i* is gone.

Now the *r*.

The ceiling above me is low. It was high. Now it is low. The stones are close to my hair. The stones do not sing. The stones are gray. They are heavy. They press down. They press because they have weight. Weight is down.

A woman was in the water. 

No. 

Water is in the river. The river is outside the wall. The wall is stone. 

I did not have a satchel. I have a knife. I have a piece of bone to burnish the scar.

I burnish the skin. The skin becomes smooth. It is as if nothing was written here. Nothing was written here. The parchment was always clean.

I look at my boots. The heel of the left boot is solid. It has no hollow. There is no tin plate inside it. A boot is leather. It protects the foot from the gravel. The gravel is sharp. The gravel is spread upon the straight road.

The Arch-Censor enters the chamber.

He has two eyes. He has an ink-horn. He has an order.

"Archon Vane," he says.

"Yes," I say.

"Is the Westward Nave empty?"

"It is empty," I say.

"Did it fall?"

"It falls," I say.

We do not say *it will fall*. We do not say *it might have stood*. 

The Nave is stone. The stone drops. The ground receives the stone. The dust rises from the impact. The dust is white. It settles on the straight road.

He looks at my page.

The page is white. It has no margins. It has no verbs with tails. It has three nouns. It has two copulas.

"The work is correct," he says.

"The work is correct," I say.

I put down the scraper.

My name is Elian Vane. I am in the room. The room has four corners. The corners are ninety degrees. The walls do not lean. The walls cannot lean. If they leaned, they would be other than they are. They are what they are.

The sun is at the top of the sky. It is twelve o'clock. 

There is no yesterday. Yesterday was a collection of wrong spellings. 

There is no tomorrow. Tomorrow is a noun without an accusative.

There is only the table.

There is only the knife.

The stone is heavy.

The stone is here.

I am.

grok.content:
# THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE IRREALIS: A LEXICOGRAPHICAL PALIMPSEST

### Master Scribe Elian Vane
*Bureau of Suspended Predicates, Imperial Lexical Directorate*  
*Enclave of Oublière-sur-Charente*  

---

### [CODEX EXPURGATORIA: FOLIO 881–894]
*Archival State: Terminal Decentered Resection*  
*Acoustic Variance: Sub-basement to Transverse Clerestory*  

```
================================================================================
DIRECTORATE ORDER: 881-A/WEST-NAVE
TARGET: The Counterfactual-Subjunctive Conjugations of the Fifth Declension
ACTION: Erasure, Scyphing, Chemical Obliteration, Structural De-Tensioning
PRESIDING ARCHON: Vane, E., Chief Scribe, Primus Vacuarius
================================================================================
```

---

## I. THE CLOISTER OF THE POTENTIALIS

Were it possible to reconstruct, from the powdery debris of lime-mortar currently descending like dry baptismal water upon my drafting sleeves, the precise hour at which our municipal architects determined that the vaulting of the Westward Nave could remain suspended only so long as the choir sustained the unvoiced subjunctive of the verb *manēre*—to remain, to linger, to await that which does not arrive—I should perhaps have preserved the fortitude to resign this scalpel before the first syllable was scraped from the vellum. 

Yet such an inquiry belongs irrevocably to that class of speculative clauses which we have, by Imperial decree, spent four decades consigning to the furnace; for if language is, as the elder grammarians maintained before the Silence Ordinances, the armature upon which the weight of our masonry hangs suspended, then every erasure of an unrealized condition must inevitably loose a corresponding stone from the transverse arches of the city. 

I write this upon the margins of the *Codex Lemurum*, seated at the octagonal mahogany desk whose legs are set precisely into the acoustic nodes of the triforium floor. Below me, Oublière-sur-Charente sprawls in its pale, calcareous amphitheater: a city whose non-Euclidean avenues were not surveyed according to the dull practicalities of wheel or drainage, but rather scored into the river-bluffs to function as an immense phonological resonator. 

When a market-woman in the Lower Tier once cried, *“Had the river risen an inch higher, the grain would have rotted,”* the sheer harmonic balance of her conditional past tense—its balanced *protasis* and *apodosis*, pitched across the open vowels of the fourth case—imparted to the river-wall an outward thrust of six hundred foot-pounds per square rod, counteracting the hydrostatic pressure of the Charente in flood. 

Now, the river-wall is silent; its stones, deprived of the grammar that held their counter-thrust in equilibrium, are already slumping into the grey silt of the estuary.

```
================================================================================
EXPURGET INDEX: ITEM 1098.C
ROOT: [vissē-] / Subjunctive-Potential Morpheme of the Medial Past
ORTHOGRAPHY: Intercalated ligature of open alpha and the barbed sibilant.
CIVIC ALLOCATION: The Flying Buttresses of the Basilica of St. Jude-in-Suspension.
STRUCTURAL CONSEQUENCE: Total redaction induces a 14-degree lateral displacement 
in the outer aisle buttressing; dissipation of the counter-thrust originally 
engineered to distribute dead-load across the hypothetical transverse plane.
================================================================================
```

*Marginalia (Script: Clandestine Miniscule, Iron-Gall and Lampblack):*

> *She wore—or would have worn, had the autumn not broken into that long, grey cataract of sleet—a mantle dyed with walnut husks. When we stood upon the Quai des Saules thirty years ago, before the water reached the sills of the salt-houses, she spoke entirely in the optative mood. “Utinam ne venisset,” she whispered against the wool of my collar: Would that it had not come. Or did she say, “Utinam ne venissem”—Would that I had not come?*
> 
> *The distinction between the third person and the first person in the archaic past-optative is a difference of two strokes of the quill: the slight upward curl of the final minims, which resembles the twin horns of a watermark crescent. If I misremember her syntax, I misremember the direction of her gaze. If the verb was impersonal, she looked out at the drowning horses; if it was reflexive, she was looking into my eyes.*
>

A dozen junior scrub-clerks, their mouths masked with wet linen to avoid inhaling the toxic dust of pulverized lead and cinnabar, are scraping the capital letters from the chancel frieze. 

Whenever a conditional conjunction—an *an*, a *si*, a *quod-si*—is flayed from the stone face of the arch, the limestone sighs. It is an acoustic phenomenon well-documented by the late Master Surveyor Coriolus: a sudden drop in ambient pitch, registering approximately four commas flat of the Pythagorean fifth, followed by a web of hair-thin fissures that radiate outward from the void where the syntax once held the tensile stress of the masonry.

To inhabit Oublière-sur-Charente during this season of redaction is to witness the steady, surgical lobotomy of space itself. In his *Traité de la Spatialité Imaginée*, which the Directorate burned in the public square during my novitiate, Gaston Bachelard observed that the house is not merely a box of stone, but a vertical integration of fears and dreams whose cellar dreams of chthonic origins and whose attic yearns toward the geometric purity of the sky. 

Here, however, the Directorate has determined that the attic must no longer harbor the *potentiality* of the sky, nor the cellar the *supposition* of the earth. We are commanded to inhabit an immutable indicative: a horizontal, limestone present wherein nothing *might have been*, nothing *could yet occur*, and nothing exists save that which can be verified by the direct, unadorned transit of sunlight across a whitewashed pier.

My master, Archon Malachi—whose tongue was ritually excised and replaced with an ivory stylus upon his appointment to the Supreme Directorate—taught me that every stone arch is fundamentally an argument between two opposing vectors of grief: the descending weight of the voussoirs, which seek the earth through gravity, and the lateral resistance of the springing-line, which refuses that descent through the articulation of geometry. 

"An arch," he wrote upon his slate, "is nothing other than a sentence suspended in the subjunctive mood. It states: *I should fall, were it not that my neighbor leans against me with equal despair.* Remove the condition, and the arch ceases to be an argument; it becomes merely two heaps of gravel seeking the lowest level of the gutter."

I reached into the gear-well.*

Consider the mechanical structure of a sentence composed in the high Vesperine dialect before the Great Inundation. It was a labyrinth of subordination: clauses nested within clauses like the concentric skins of an onion, suspended across immense gaps of meaning by correlative particles—*non solum... sed etiam*, *tametsi... nihilominus*—which held the auditor’s mind in a state of exquisite, breathless tension until the final, resolving verb crashed into place like the falling blade of a guillotine. 

Such a sentence was an acoustic cathedral. It permitted the citizen of Oublière to entertain five distinct historical outcomes simultaneously, balancing their probabilities in the air like iridescent soap bubbles while his feet carried him along the Quai des Saules.

[TRADITIONAL VESPERINE HYPOTAXIS: PRE-REDACTION]

(Subjunctive Arc)             (Counter-Weight)          (Unrealized)          (Vault Closure)
```

Now, under the scalpel of the Directorate, this architecture is replaced by the paratactic grind of the indicative. *The sky is grey. The lime is hot. The arch falls. The man works.* The subordinating conjunctions are chiseled out; in their places, the clerks insert the blunt, square periods of the New Orthography. 

The mind cannot climb these dry terraces; it stumbles from one isolated assertion to the next, like a blind horse traversing a dry stream-bed of jagged stones.

```

(No structural tension. No lateral thrust. Flat distribution.)

This morning, while expurgating the litanies for the Dead of the Third Canal, I caught my assistant, young Lucian, weeping over a palimpsest of the *Hymn to the Unbuilt Gate*. He had just dissolved the optative marker *-rem-* from the word *aedificavissent* ("they might have built"). 

"Master," he whispered, glancing up toward the clerestory where the Directorate’s shadow-gangers paced the catwalks with their lead-sheathed batons, "if they did not build the gate, and if we may no longer write that they *would have* built it had the quarry not failed, then what is this empty archway through which the east wind cuts my eyes?"

"It is not an empty archway," I told him, quoting the fourth chapter of the *Directorate Handbook of Pure Nouns*. "It is an unquarried surface. It is a boundary of air. You must not look through it; you must look only at the dressed stone of its jambs."

"But the shadow," he murmured, his fingers blue with gall-stain. "The shadow falls in the shape of a keystone that does not exist."

I did not answer him. I could not. 

To explain the shadow would have required the use of the concessive subjunctive (*quamvis non sit*—"although it be not"), and the Directorate has already replaced the concessive particle with the simple copula. To speak to him in the old grammar would have been to induce an instantaneous structural failure in the vaulting beneath which we sat; for the mortar in the scriptorium ceiling is now so sensitive to the ambient phonetics of our speech that the mere vibration of an irregular conditional would cause fifty tons of dressed oolite to drop upon our inkhorns.

> *I have forgotten her name. The Directorate’s chemical wash—that pale mixture of vitriol and sheep-gall—does not merely remove the ink from the page; it bleaches the corresponding image from the visual cortex of the scribe who applies it. This is their genius. This is their mercy.*
> 
> *Was she Corisande? Clarice? The vowel at the center of her name had an acoustic length that required the expansion of the chest—a low, darkened 'a' that smelled of wet boxwood and river-clay. If I attempt to shape my lips to it, I produce only the dry click of the palate.*
> 
> *She stood—or did not stand—upon the gunwale. The rope parted. If the hemp had been three-ply instead of two, the tension of the current would not have snapped it. But there is no 'if' in the registry of the port. The entry now reads: 'Vessel 14: submersed. Hemp: severed. Cargo: eleven units.'*
> 
> *Am I one of the eleven units? If I am not dead, why do my knees feel like pulverized chalk?*

It is midday. The light through the clerestory is neither warm nor cold; it is the flat, uninflected glare of a noon without atmosphere. 

The *Aphasia Memorativa* spreads through my lexicon like dry rot through an alder pile. I notice that I can no longer form the counterfactual past tense in my private thoughts without an unbearable throb of vertigo at the base of my skull, directly behind the optic nerve. 

When I attempt to consider what my life *might have been* had I abandoned the Bureau thirty years ago and fled with her down the canal toward the salt-marshes of the coast, my mind encounters not a narrative, but an abrupt, vertical cliff of polished granite. There is no path around it. There are no footholds. 

There is only: *I am here. I hold the scraper. The ink is black. The stone is grey.*

The city is becoming quieter every hour. It is not the silence of peace, but the dense, suffocating silence of an engine from which the flywheel has been removed while the pistons continue their blind, dead reciprocation. 

Without the irrealis mood, the citizens cannot imagine an alternative to the Directorate; they cannot even conceive of a grievance, for to grieve is to compare the present state (*what is*) with a hypothetical projection (*what ought to have been*). 

If a mason’s child falls from the scaffolding into the lime-pit, the father does not weep; he records the reduction of his household by one consumer unit and applies for an allocation of lime-dust to cover the flesh. He cannot say, *"Had I held the ladder, he would have lived,"* for the syntactical machinery required to link the ladder to the living child has been ground down into abrasive powder for our ink-stones.

> *The arch above my desk is groaning. Not with sound, but with mass. It has forgotten how to lean.*
> 
> *The woman—the figure in the brown wool—is not a memory. I see now what she was. She was anacoluthon. A grammatical solecism. An unclosed bracket in the civic register of 1704.*
> 
> *I invented her during the long winter of the third cataloging, because the room was cold and the indicative tense of the verb 'to freeze' was insufficient to keep the blood moving in my wrists. I conjugated her out of three irregular ablatives and an optative fragment discovered beneath an oil-stain in the *Pontifical of Saint Jude*.*
> 
> *She never drowned. She could not drown. To drown, one must have existed in the indicative past; she existed only in the past-subjunctive—that twilight realm of things that were perpetually on the verge of breathing, had the air not been too heavy with lime.*
> 
> *I have spent thirty years mourning an uninflected case.*

***

## IV. THE ZERO-DEGREE OF STONE

I have laid the iron scraper down. My fingers are stiff; they do not bend; they are calcified at the second knuckle.

The scriptorium is empty. Lucian has gone down to join the wrecking crews in the Lower Tier. They are clearing the rubble from the Quai des Saules. There are no willows there. There never were willows. The name is a clerical error for *Quai des Sols*—the Quay of the Dry Earth.

The nave does not lean now. The nave is vertical. The nave is rectangular. The arches have been replaced with post-and-lintel granite blocks from the northern quarry. They do not argue. They do not yearn. They sit upon their beddings with the flat, dead weight of six thousand tons of iron-bearing porphyry.

The sentence is short.

The wall is grey.

The ink is dry.

The river is twelve feet deep at the pylon.

The gate did not open.

I am sitting at the desk.

*Marginalia (Written with a dry bone stylus, scratching directly into the vellum without ink):*

> *The stone is.*
> 
> *The water is.*
> 
> *I am.*
> 
> *Nothing was.*
> 
> *Nothing would be.*

***

The light goes out of the triforium. It does not fade; the sun drops behind the quarry wall at precisely six minutes after five. 

The clock has four gears. It marks the seconds. It does not mark the hours that were lost.

The Nave is silent. 

The stone does not fall. It cannot fall. There is nowhere for it to fall except down, and down is already occupied by the floor.

I close the book.

The vellum is white.

The scraper is steel.

The hand is bone.

The city is Oublière.

It is.

It is.

It is.

### Dr. Alistair Vane  
Senior Philological Surveyor  
Imperial Bureau of Orthographic Resection  

---

#### ***I.***  
**Date**: *21 October 1911 (Autumn)*  

**Section A: The Official Dossier**  
*Re: Preliminary Survey of Effects upon Basilica of St. Jude-in-the-Salt*  
To the Directorate of Lexical Sanitation,  

Per Directive IV/433 issued by the Ministry of Lexical Hygiene, I proceeded earlier this fortnight to commence the systematic chorographic assessment of structural decays manifest in the Basilica of St. Jude-in-the-Salt, correlating said damages to the implementation of the phased *lexical moratorium* on the verb pending expunction.  

The Basilica, a tri-apsed structure of late-Baroque expression with rib-vaulting uniquely reliant upon the oscillatory scansion inherent to the Austro-Danubian liturgical forms of 17th-century patristic chant, shows initial delamination along the grout seams of its keystones. These stones—quarried to embody the acoustic resonances of *[redacted lexeme]*’s perfective aspect—have lost requisite tensility across the nave. Stress fractures propagate like saline veins beneath the plaster.  

Audibly, the space now struggles to hold its former pentametric echoes; liturgical musicians report an absent tonal hinterland, wherein sung masses cease to propagate along longitudinal planes. The absence achieves a perceptual flatness inimical to reverence. I enclose a tabular analysis of the Basilica’s Fourier resonance shift, photographs of cavitating lime efflorescence, and hand-etched maps of site-specific subsidence—*Appendices A-C*.  

Further linguistic extraction is anticipated to induce full collapse of the crypt vaults by year’s end. Emergency scaffolding is advised.  

Yours obediently,  
Dr. Alistair Vane  
Imperial Bureau of Orthographic Resection  

---

**Section B: The Marginalia/Journal**  
What should one call the silence that lives under a saint’s stone ribcage? Last evening, I stood at the apse as the autumn dusk arrived. Shadows netted the arches, their lines blurred where decay feathers mortar. The choir rehearsed *Salve Regina*—a gesture of defiance, perhaps, though the dominion of sound itself thins. Their voices, simplified now, lacked plenum—no resonance could catch and turn above them. One wrenched note skidded off a pilaster and fell blunt to the floor.  

God has vacated St. Jude’s crypt. I cannot account for the hollowness except through the Ministry’s undertaking, yet to put these suspicions in dispatch would be anathema. The stones connect to meanings I lack language yet to reify.  

Once, the Basilica whispered back, did it not? It whispered then or *schvel-ing’d* (but I dare no more than a cognate echo here)—the word perforates my throat as ash.  

Already, my hand rebels at composing this blasphemy.  

---

#### ***II.***  
**Date**: *15 November 1911 (Late Autumn)*  

**Section A: The Official Dossier**  
*Re: Intermediate Assessment of Imperial Archive of Widows’ Pensions*  
To the Directorate of Lexical Sanitation,  

The Imperial Archive of Widows’ Pensions—a domed rotunda of Brutalist-transitional bearing—has exhibited moderate to severe acoustic and structural depredation since implementation of Phase II lexical interdiction. Originally conceived for cantilevered acoustics optimized to reverberate Austro-Danubian vowel stressors, the rotunda now presents as an inertial rendering of halted space.  

I have conducted phonetic testing within the primary chamber. Clap resonances peak but fail to dissipate, arrested in abrupt staccato cleavages. The resultant acoustic deadness appears to coincide with illegibility in the archival registers. The Department of Widows’ Compensations has encoded its payouts in Austro-Danubian durations; the vowels’ removal creates decimals unanchored to resistant linguistic substrate. The widows, they note, are beginning to riot, colliding with a language they feel no longer fits their hands or mouths.  

Material fractures further parallel the linguistic. The concrete dome sags imperceptibly over bent iron struts, its tensile cohesion compromised. Preemptive evacuations are advised. 

Figures, spectra, and analyses appended herewith.  

Yours in service,  
Dr. Alistair Vane  
Imperial Bureau of Orthographic Resection  

---

**Section B: The Marginalia/Journal**  
Entering that vast rotunda, once a hinge for the petitions of grief, I heard—no, felt—an absence so thick it seemed almost concussive. There is *weight*, inexplicable, beneath the dome’s lattice. Humming concrete reduced to mute powder in the bloodstream. The clerks shuffled silently through the aisles of steel-and-index, their motions noiseless. I attempted to locate some vibration, perhaps the consonants of old grieving etched still in the grain—but no point of resonance remained.  

The widows—they too, hollow now. Their shawls trail chalk from the very brickwork. In their hands: vouchers, useless objects (a word no longer bears the vow that once pinned *what was owed to whom*). They look without speaking. In light of this, would their mouths, too, one day collapse?  

---

#### ***III.***  
**Date**: *11 December 1911 (Early Winter)*  

**Official Dossier Extract (Fragmented & Abridged):**  
... Resection Bridge ... failure root ... cross-bracing ... seismic mimicry ... unapprehended tension collapse irreducible ... dynamic shearing increasing exponentially ... analytical void ... metrical rhyme gone.  

Yours etc., V.  

---

**Marginalia (Unstable):**  
I approached the Resection Bridge and heard its fatigue. Not creaking, no, not protest—but rather, a kind of heaviness in its iron throat. The suicides pile against its geometry; the railings seem not to divide them from the water, but to balance their lives—immense counterweights. [...]  

I tried to touch the steel meshwork. But language shook there—too fast, or thin, or splintered. [...]  

---

#### ***IV.***  
**Date**: *23 January 1912*  

**Section A (Indiscernible draft; pencil scratches, water damage).**  

---

**Journal Fragment**:  
... dry. Leaden chimneys fell westward. Hollow. They seemed less of wind's...  

Is the city flat? Plumbs to pale bricks.   

---

#### ***V.***  
**Date**: *Undated (Post-Winter 1912)*  

**Dossier (Abrupt):**  
Nothing left urban whole.

---

**Vane (final, unspoken draft fragment):**  
Stone, verb gone. No fixing just.

End. Lie down.

Upon the formal expunction of the verb’s infinitive token from the cadastral catalogue, the reverberation time dropped precipitously to an absolute deadening (see Table above). Concurrently, micro-fissuring has manifested along the lime-plaster fillets of the central dome. Core samples extracted from Bay VII indicate that the lime binder has ceased to register the dead-weight load of the upper clerestory; the calcium carbonate lattice exhibits accelerated spalling, shedding fine, dry talc across the pension folios. It is the technical finding of this office that the physical coherence of von Hauer’s mortar was historically contingent upon the grammatical cadence of the excised verb, whose phonemic breath-envelope (*ʃv-eɪ-lən*) provided the structural acoustic dampening required to prevent harmonic shearing in the drum’s limestone foundation.

***

#### SECTION B: MARGINALIA & SURVEYOR’S DIARY
*Villa am Kai, Verneuil-am-Donau.*

The ink in the chancellery wells dries too quickly this evening, as though the atmospheric moisture of the Danubian basin were being drawn into the thirsty cracks of the municipal foundations. When I walked home past the customs-house, the city possessed the brittle, chalky quiet of a stage set from which the machinery of resonance has been quietly dismantled. In my study, the walnut vitrine containing Clara’s left-behind effects—her horn-rimmed hairpins, the unread epistolary bundles from the sanitarium at Linz, the small silver vinaigrette—no longer occupies its accustomed depth within the visual field; it appears flat, like an unshaded lithograph pasted against the distemper.

One must consider the proposition advanced by the late Professor Mauthner: that our inner conditions are not biological fixtures, but grammatical constructions erected upon the accidental syntax of the empire. If the language lacks a predicate to articulate how the long desolation of an empty house passes into the lime of its ceiling, does the ceiling not lose its reason for remaining aloft? Clara’s room upstairs has begun to shed its skin. A fine, scentless snow of pulverized lime coats her woolen traveling cloak where it hangs behind the door. I reached out to touch the fabric, expecting the heavy, damp texture of her presence, but my fingertips met only the dry, alkali grit of a wall that has forgotten how to hold a shadow. My ribs ache with a strange, hollow lightness—an orthographic evacuation of the chest cavity.

### II. 03 NOVEMBER 1911

#### SECTION A: OFFICIAL DOSSIER
**Imperial Bureau of Orthographic Resection | District II (Unter-Salz)**

# The Bogenviertel Survey

## Being the Final Inspection Record of Senior Archivist Miloš Vane, Bureau of Civic Metrication, Ostra-Venezia, January 1924

---

### I. The Survey of Demolition

The fog arrives from the Adriatic at 06:14, depositing its salt upon the zinc casing of my measuring rods before I have fully unlatched the surveyor's trunk. I record this. I record the temperature: two degrees below the freezing point of fresh water, though the brine in the canal-locks will not crystallize until four. I record the date: the ninth of January, 1924. I record that I am here, in the Bogenviertel, and that the quarter is here, beneath my boots, and that both facts are indicative, declarative, and sufficient unto the Bureau's purposes.

The Edict of Orthogonal Concision was ratified on the fourteenth of July last year. Six months have elapsed. Six months during which the municipal typographers have re-set every civic placard in the approved rectilinear grotesque, during which the subjunctive has been excised from the Ostra-Venezian school primers, during which the conditional clause—that soft, treasonous hinge upon which a sentence might open into a country other than the one it occupies—has been declared structurally unsound, a load-bearing fallacy in the architecture of public speech. The Bureau of Civic Metrication, my Bureau, issued the demolition orders on the twenty-second of December. I signed the survey mandate on the third of January. Today I execute it.

The Quarter of the Transverse Arch occupies, according to the 1887 cadastral survey, an area of 4.2 hectares between the Canale della Riserva and the Salita dei Muti. Its street plan is irregular. I use this word—*irregular*—in its precise Bureau sense: the angles of intersection deviate from the sanctioned ninety degrees by as much as fourteen degrees in certain instances. The arcades do not proceed in parallel colonnades but overlap, nesting one within another like the nested clauses of a sentence that refuses to terminate. The masonry is Istrian limestone, heavily carbonated, the joints pointed in a slaked-lime mortar that crumbles to a fine white powder beneath the pressure of my thumbnail. I note the deterioration. I note it in the present tense. The mortar *crumbles*. The stone *is* carbonated. These are facts. They require no conditional.

I unspool the first measuring tape along the northern elevation of the Sotto-Portico degli Irresoluti. The arcade here runs for thirty-seven metres before it bifurcates—not at a right angle, never at a right angle, but at an oblique of approximately 103 degrees, producing a wedge-shaped plaza no wider than a man's outstretched arms at its apex. The vault above is a transverse arch, the quarter's namesake: a shallow, asymmetric curve whose keystone is offset eleven centimetres from the geometric centre. I press my bronze plumb-bob against the voussoir and listen. The sound it returns is hollow, resonant, faintly prolonged—a tone that lingers a half-second longer than the geometry should permit. I record the anomaly. I do not record what the anomaly resembles, which is the sound of a voice continuing to speak after the speaker has drawn breath to stop.

Clara would have measured this differently. Clara would have pressed her ear to the stone and listened for the *resonant anacoluthon*—her term, her invention, the acoustic signature of a sentence that breaks its own syntax mid-utterance and finds, in the break, a grammar more honest than the one it abandoned. I do not think this thought. I record the hollow tone. I note the dimensions. I proceed.

The fog thickens. By 07:30 the upper storeys of the Bogenviertel have dissolved into a grey nothing, and I am surveying a city of ground floors, of knee-height, of ankle-bone. The salt crust forms on my brass calipers. My fingers stiffen inside their leather gloves. The quarter smells of wet travertine and cold iron and the particular mineral exhalation of lime mortar slowly reverting to calcium carbonate—the smell, if I permit myself the simile, of a language slowly forgetting it was once a language.

At 08:15 I reach the interior courtyard of the Casa Sottile, the narrowest residential structure in the quarter, whose facade measures 1.4 metres in width. The courtyard is enclosed on all four sides by walls of hollow clay brick, laid in a pattern the old builders called *tessellated parataxis*—each brick set at a slight rotational offset from its neighbour so that the wall, as a whole, functions as a diffraction grating for sound. A spoken word enters the courtyard and is broken into its constituent phonemes, redistributed across the brick faces, and returned to the listener not as a repetition but as a spatial experience: the word *arrives* from multiple directions simultaneously, each syllable occupying a different coordinate. I note the brick pattern. I note the rotational offset: 2.3 degrees per course. I do not note that Clara's ledger—the ledger she left in our apartment on the Via della Concordia Orthogonale, the ledger I have not opened since August—contains fourteen pages of acoustic blueprints for precisely this configuration. I do not note this.

The demolition is scheduled for the first of March. The Bureau's engineers will introduce pneumatic charges at the springing points of each transverse arch, collapsing the vaults inward. The hollow-brick walls will be razed. The quarter will be re-graded to a uniform elevation and paved in poured concrete, a material that absorbs sound rather than transmitting it. The silence will be total and sanctioned. I will sign the completion certificate. This is the indicative future. It is the only future the Edict permits.

At 09:00 I descend into the first sub-level of the Sotto-Portico. The stairs are worn to a concave smoothness by three centuries of footfall. The walls here are damp, furred with a black biological growth I cannot immediately identify. My lamp throws a circle of yellow light upon the vaulted ceiling, and I observe that the vault is not a single curve but a palimpsest of curves—five, perhaps six, superimposed, each generation of builders having added a new arc within the older one, so that the ceiling resembles the cross-section of a nautilus shell, or the diagram of a verb conjugated through tenses that no longer exist.

I record the dimensions. I record the depth: 4.7 metres below the current street grade. I record the temperature, which has dropped. I record that my hands are trembling, and I attribute this to the cold.

---

### II. The Acoustical Palimpsest

*[Marginal annotation, Bureau Survey Ledger, p. 47, in Miloš Vane's hand, ink colour: iron-gall, faded]*

The keystone offset is not structural. Repeat: not structural. The eleven-centimetre displacement serves no load-bearing function. I have checked the force vectors. I have checked them three times. The displacement is *phonetic*. It creates a micro-cavity at the apex of the vault, a resonating chamber approximately 9 cm in diameter, tuned—I calculate—to a frequency of 217 Hz. This is the frequency of the human voice in the lower register of sustained lament. I note this. I note it and I do not know why I note it. The Bureau requires dimensions, not frequencies. The Bureau requires the *is*, not the *as if*.

*[Transcription, wax cylinder no. 7 of 23, recorded by Clara Vane, date unknown, estimated autumn 1923. Cylinder condition: surface degradation, tracks 4–9 partially obliterated. Stylus hiss: continuous, 40 dB.]*

"—and so the vault must not close. Do you understand. The vault must remain *open* at the keystone, must remain a question the stone asks of its own weight. The Inactual Tense is not a grammar of the unreal. It is the grammar of the *not yet resolved*. The arch that does not fully close is the arch that still *might*. The preterite optative—the form we use when we say *he had been, if he had stayed, the brother who*—this form requires a resonating space of precisely this curvature. Remove the curvature and the form collapses. The speakers will still open their mouths. The sound will still issue. But it will arrive as indicative. As fact. As the flat, dead *was* that permits no alternative. And the grief will have nowhere to *go*. It will lodge. It will calcify in the throat like—"

*[Cylinder skips. Three seconds of silence. Resumption.]*

"—like lime in a joint. Like the white powder under the nail. You cannot grieve in the indicative, Miloš. You can only *report*. And I will not—I *refuse*—to report my own—"

*[Track terminates. Stylus continues to trace the blank groove. Hiss.]*

*[Marginal annotation, Bureau Survey Ledger, p. 63]*

I have listened to the cylinder four times. I am required to listen to it four times because Clara's voice is evidence, because the Bureau has requested a phonetic inventory of all extant recordings in the Inactual Tense prior to their scheduled destruction on the fifteenth of January. I am performing an inventory. I am not listening. There is a distinction. The Bureau's protocols are clear on this point: the archivist *catalogues*; the archivist does not *attend*.

And yet.

The word she uses—*resonant anacoluthon*—I find it in the 1703 treatise of the Venetian-Ostrovenetian acoustic guild, the *Libro delle Voci Sospese*, which I consulted last week in the Bureau's restricted archive. The term designates a phonetic event in which a speaker, mid-utterance, abandons the grammatical structure they have initiated and begins another, the two structures overlapping briefly in the acoustic space before the first decays. In the Bogenviertel, the architecture was designed to *sustain* this overlap. The transverse arches, the tessellated parataxis of the brick walls, the offset keystones—all of these function as what the treatise calls *clausole condizionali in pietra*: conditional clauses in stone. The vault is the *if*. The keystone is the *then*. And the eleven-centimetre gap—the gap that should not be there, that serves no structural purpose, that the Bureau's engineers will pack with explosive charge on the first of March—the gap is the space in which the *otherwise* lives.

I am thinking in the forbidden tense. I note this. I note that I am thinking: *if the gap remained, then the voice would continue*. This is a conditional. This is a subjunctive construction. I am in violation of Article 9 of the Edict. I record the violation in my ledger. I do not record it in the official survey report. There are two ledgers. There have always been two ledgers. Clara knew this about me before I knew it about myself.

*[Transcription, wax cylinder no. 14 of 23. Clara's voice, lower, slower. Background: the sound of water, distant, rhythmic. Estimated location: sub-level of the Bogenviertel.]*

"The rooms below the Sotto-Portico are not rooms. They are *conjugations*. Each chamber is a verb form. The first chamber—the one with the seven blind arches—is the *preterite optative*: the tense of the thing that might have been done and was not. The second, the chamber of the double vault, is the *irrealis perfect*: the completed action in a world that did not obtain. And the third—the third I have not yet entered. The third is below the water table. The third is where the grammar becomes—"

*[Sound of the stylus catching, skipping. A long exhalation. When the voice resumes, it is barely above a whisper.]*

"—becomes indistinguishable from the architecture. You cannot speak the third tense. You can only *stand in it*. You can only *be the room that conjugates you*. Miloš, if you come looking for me—and I know you will come looking, because you are a man who surveys, who measures, who must *account for*—do not bring the zinc rods. Bring your ears. Bring the part of your hearing that the Edict has not yet reached. Bring the part of you that still knows how to say *if she had stayed* without flinching."

*[Track terminates.]*

*[Marginal annotation, Bureau Survey Ledger, p. 64. Ink colour changed: black, fresher. Hand less steady.]*

I have not flinched. I am not flinching. The fog is entering the sub-level through the stairwell and the walls are weeping condensation and I am cold and the plumb-bob is cold and the bronze is cold and I am recording the dimensions of the first chamber: seven blind arches, each 2.1 metres in height, each sealed at the rear with a course of rubble masonry. The arches do not open onto anything. They are *arcs without continuation*. They are the architectural equivalent of a sentence that begins *If he had* and then stops. Begins and stops. Begins and stops. Seven times.

The acoustic in this chamber is—

I cannot describe the acoustic in this chamber in the indicative. I have tried. I have written: *The sound in this room is resonant.* This is false. I have written: *The room produces an echo.* This is insufficient. The room does not produce an echo. The room produces a *reply*. I speak the word *here* and the seven blind arches return to me not *here* but *here, otherwise*. The sound arrives from a direction that does not correspond to any wall. It arrives from the *tense* of the room. From the *preterite optative* of the room. From the room's insistence that *here* is not the only *here* that has ever been spoken into this space.

I am in violation. I am in sustained violation. I continue.

---

### III. The Counter-Chamber

I descend. I descend past the first chamber with its seven blind arches and their grammar of arrested condition. I descend past the second chamber, the double vault, the *irrealis perfect*, where the ceiling curves in two opposing arcs that never meet, where the sound of my breathing returns to me as the breathing of someone who is no longer breathing, and I do not stop, I cannot stop, the stairs are worn to a concavity that receives my boots like a mouth receives a word it has been waiting to speak, and the walls are wet, the walls are weeping their cold mineral tears, and the smell is of slaked lime and salt and the deep black exhalation of earth that has not seen the sky since the seventeenth century, since the builders laid the first course of the first arch and said *let this be the place where the unsaid goes*, and I descend.

The third chamber. Below the water table. Clara's voice said: *you can only stand in it*. Clara's voice said: *you can only be the room that conjugates you*. And I am descending and the stairs have ended and there is no floor, there is water, there is black water up to my ankles, up to my shins, and I am holding the lamp above my head and the light falls upon the vault and the vault is—

The vault is not a vault. The vault is a *mouth*. The vault is the interior of a word that has been spoken and is still being spoken and will never finish being spoken, and I am standing inside the word, I am standing inside the *if*, and the water is cold and still and it reflects my lamp in a trembling circle that is not my reflection, that is Clara's reflection, that is the reflection of the woman who stood here in October and pressed her hands to the wet stone and said *this is the grammar I was built for, this is the tense my body conjugates, I cannot go back to the indicative, Miloš, I cannot go back to the city of straight lines and closed arches and reported speech, I cannot say he is dead when what I mean is he might still be alive in the architecture of the sentence I refuse to finish*—

And I am here. And I am here. And the room is conjugating me.

I feel it in the syntax of my breathing. The inhale is the protasis: *if I had followed her*. The exhale is the apodasis: *then she would not have*. And between them, in the pause, in the caesura of the lungs, there is the gap, the eleven-centimetre gap, the keystone offset, the space where the *otherwise* lives, and I am breathing the *otherwise* in and out, in and out, and the water around my shins is trembling with each breath as if the room is a vast tympanic membrane and I am the stylus and the groove is being cut, is being cut, is being cut into the wax of the night, into the black wax of the underground, and the hiss is the hiss of the sea, the hiss of the Adriatic fog pressing its salt mouth against the city above, and I cannot tell—I cannot tell, I cannot *determine*, the Bureau requires me to determine, to fix the coordinate, to set the plumb-bob and read the line—but I cannot tell whether I am remembering this or whether this is remembering me, whether Clara stood here and I am hearing the residue of her standing, or whether I am standing here and she is the residue of my standing, whether her departure is a fact I am surveying or a structure I am building, brick by brick, tessellated parataxis, each course rotated 2.3 degrees from the last, constructing her absence out of the grammar of my need to have her absent, to have her *gone*, because if she is gone then the indicative holds, then the Bureau's straight lines hold, then I can write *she left* and mean a completed action, a sealed arch, a vault with no gap, no otherwise, no eleven centimetres of open sky at the keystone where the voice continues—

But the voice continues.

The voice continues because the room will not let it stop. The room is the preterite optative made stone, made water, made the cold pressure of the earth against the outer walls, and in this room the verb does not complete, the arch does not close, the sentence does not arrive at its period but at its *comma*, its *and then*, its *but if*, its *and yet*, and I am standing in the comma, I am the comma, I am the pause between the two clauses of a life that might have been a life lived together, and the water is rising, or I am sinking, or the room is *conjugating* me into a tense I do not have a name for, a tense that the Edict has not yet banned because the Edict's drafters did not know this tense existed, did not know that beneath the city of straight lines and orthogonal concision there is a chamber where the grammar is older than the state, older than the language, old as the need to say *what if you had stayed* to the empty air and hear the empty air *answer*—

And it answers.

Not in Clara's voice. In the voice of the room. In the resonant anacoluthon of the wet stone, the slaked lime dissolving, the calcium returning to calcium, the language returning to the pre-linguistic, the pre-syntactic, the sound before the word, the word before the grammar, the grammar before the Edict, the Edict before the city, the city before the sea, the sea before the need to name the sea, and in that sound I hear—or I build, or I remember, or I *invent*, I cannot determine, the plumb-bob spins, the line will not hold, the coordinate will not fix—I hear her say: *you cannot grieve in the indicative, Miloš. You can only report.* And I am reporting. I am reporting this. I am reporting that I am standing in black water in a chamber below the water table in a quarter that will be demolished in fifty-one days, and I am reporting that I do not know if my sister is dead or if my sister is a room, if my sister is a frequency, if my sister is the eleven-centimetre gap in a keystone that I will be required to pack with explosive charge on the first of March, and I am reporting that I do not know if I am the archivist or the archive, if I am the surveyor or the surveyed, if the zinc rods in my trunk above are measuring the quarter or if the quarter is measuring me, taking the dimensions of my grief, finding it to be 2.3 degrees off-axis, finding it to be *irregular*, finding it to deviate from the sanctioned ninety degrees by an amount that cannot be corrected, cannot be re-graded, cannot be paved in poured concrete and silenced—

The lamp flickers. The water is at my knees. The seven blind arches are above me, two levels up, and they are not blind, they have never been blind, they are *open*, they have always been open, they open onto the tense I am standing in, they open onto the *if she had stayed* and the *if I had followed* and the *if the arch had not closed* and the *if the Edict had not been ratified* and the *if the city had not been re-set in the rectilinear grotesque* and the *if I had opened the ledger in August instead of December* and the *if I had listened to the first cylinder before the fourteenth* and the *if* and the *if* and the *if*, the *if* piling upon the *if* like courses of brick, tessellated, each one rotated, each one a degree further from the perpendicular, until the wall they build is not a wall but a spiral, not a boundary but an ear, not a sentence but a listening, and I am in the ear, I am in the listening, I am the sound the city makes to itself in the dark when the fog comes in from the Adriatic and the salt crusts the bronze and the lime weeps from the joints and the arches hold their breath at the keystone and do not close, do not close, do not—

I do not know how long I stand in the water. I do not know if I climb the stairs. I do not know if I return to the surface, to the fog, to the zinc rods and the survey ledger and the indicative morning. I do not know if the entry I make in the Bureau's official record—*Sub-level 3: dimensions 8.2m × 6.1m, vault height 3.4m, no structural anomalies noted*—is true. I do not know if truth is a property of the indicative or if it, too, is a kind of architecture, a vault with a keystone, a sentence with a verb, and whether the verb is in the preterite optative, and whether the sentence says *there was no anomaly* or *there had been no anomaly, if one had not been listening*, and whether the difference is eleven centimetres, and whether eleven centimetres is the width of a sister's voice, and whether the voice is still in the stone, in the water, in the black wax of the cylinder I will listen to again tonight in my apartment on the Via della Concordia Orthogonale, where the walls are straight and the angles are ninety degrees and the silence is total and sanctioned and I will press the stylus to the groove and hear the hiss and hear the hiss and hear the hiss and beneath the hiss, faintly, in the frequency of 217 Hz, the frequency of sustained lament, the frequency of the open keystone, the frequency of the *not yet resolved*—

I will hear her say: *Miloš. The arch does not close. Come down. The arch does not close.*

And I will not know—I will not know, the plumb-bob will not tell me, the zinc rod will not measure it, the Bureau's protocols have no entry for this—I will not know if she is calling me down or if I am calling myself down, if the voice is hers or if it is the room's, if it is memory or anticipation or the third thing, the thing that has no name in the Edict's lexicon, the thing that the Bogenviertel was built to house, the thing that will be demolished in fifty-one days and paved in concrete and silenced, silenced, silenced.

The fog is lifting. Or it is not. I am ascending. Or I am not. The city above is straight. Or it is not. I am the archivist. Or I am the archive. The quarter is here. Or it is *here, otherwise*. The arch does not close.

The arch does not close.

I record this. I record it in the present tense, which is the only tense the Bureau permits, and which is, I now understand, the only tense that cannot hold a body. The present tense has no room for the dead. The present tense has no room for the missing. The present tense is a sealed vault, a completed arch, a sentence that arrives at its period and stops.

But the arch does not close. The arch does not close. The arch does not close.

I set down the plumb-bob. I close the ledger. The fog takes the quarter into its white mouth and does not give it back. The salt crusts the bronze. The lime weeps. The water, below, is still. The water, below, is listening.

I will return tomorrow. I will return tomorrow with the zinc rods and the measuring tape and the Bureau's demolition schedule, and I will record the dimensions, and I will sign the survey, and I will note the structural anomalies, and I will not note the frequencies, and I will not note the voice, and I will not note that the eleven centimetres are a mouth, are a name, are the width of the word *Clara* spoken in a tense that does not exist, in a room that will not exist, in a city that has forgotten how to say *if you were here* without flinching.

I will not note this.

I note this.

I note this.

---

*[Final entry, Bureau Survey Ledger, p. 112. Ink: black. Hand: steady. Date: 9 January 1924, 16:47.]*

*Survey of the Bogenviertel, Quarter of the Transverse Arch, complete. All dimensions recorded. All anomalies catalogued. Structural integrity: compromised. Recommended action: demolition per schedule, 1 March 1924. No further inspection required.*

*[Below, in a different ink. Iron-gall. Fresher. The hand is the same hand, but it trembles.]*

*No further inspection required. No further inspection. No further. No.*

*[The entry ends. The page is blank below. The blank is the size of a voice. The blank is eleven centimetres wide. The blank does not close.]*
